title: Nodes · what I built and what I found · Mark Martin

slides.name: Cover · Nodes

params.text: A teaching model, an app, and what the evidence said
What 5,003 examiner findings reveal about how students think, and the app I built to act on it.
Assistant Professor, Computer Science & Education Practice

slides.notes:
OPEN with the room, not the slide: "Hands up if you've marked an answer and thought: they KNOW this. So why didn't they get the marks?"

This talk is two things: an app I built, Nodes, and what I found when I read every examiner report I could get my hands on.

Don't introduce yourself here. The poll comes first.

Who's telling the story: a teacher first.

The question that started it came from marking: students who clearly knew the content, losing the marks anyway. Bridge to the next slide.

params.text:
They know the content.
They still lose the marks.

slides.notes:
Let this sit. One question drives everything that follows.

"I built a teaching model to answer it, then an app to act on the answer, then went looking for evidence that would tell me if I was right."

slides.name: The research question

params.text: What can examination questions, mark schemes and examiner reports across education systems reveal about the reasoning students are expected to show, the relationships their answers fail to establish, and the support that might help them progress?

layers.name: What is missing, and what st

params.text: What is missing, and what stays uncertain

layers.name: What a student can do alone,

params.text: What a student can do alone, prompted, hinted, and in a new task

layers.name: Nodes does not map how the m

params.text: Nodes does not map how the mind thinks. It maps how thinking is demanded, rewarded and observed in examination evidence, and turns that into teaching hypotheses to test with students.

slides.notes:
The question the whole project is built around. Read it slowly.

Five sources of evidence, read in turn: what the question requires, what the mark scheme credits, what examiners describe, what that means and what stays uncertain, and only then what to teach.

Then the stance, which I keep throughout: this is not a map of the mind. It's a map of how thinking is demanded, rewarded and observed, and every teaching move is a hypothesis to test.

slides.name: Act 01 · What I built

layers.name: An app that treats every que

params.text: An app that treats every question as a network of small capabilities, and every answer as evidence about each one.

slides.notes: Act one: the build. Keep it brisk: three slides, then the evidence.

slides.name: Every question is a network

params.text:
Every question is
a network of nodes
Each node is one capability the question demands. Its number is the model’s estimate from the answers recorded, allowing for a slip or a lucky guess: a map of demands, not of the mind.

slides.notes:
The core idea of Nodes. A question like "Explain how a larger cache improves performance" isn't one skill: it's recall, understanding, connecting, applying, qualifying, transferring.

Each node holds a belief, the chance the student can do it. Every answer updates those beliefs (knowledge tracing), allowing for slips and lucky guesses.

The percentages here are illustrative, not data.

slides.notes:
Six frameworks: Computer Science GCSE, Singapore O-Level computing, Gaokao IT, and three of my own models (critical text, technical analysis, the growth model).

58 stages in all. Each stage is a question with five tabs: what to recall first, the question itself, how to answer it, how it's marked, and the analysis for teachers.

The screenshot is the live site.

slides.name: Four lenses on every stage

params.text: Colour by: Backbone · Bloom · Cognitive · Mastery
Our five kinds of thinking: U A C X J
The process exercised: retrieval to transfer

slides.notes:
The header switch, "Colour by", recolours every diagram in the app through one of four lenses. These are the Fingerprints: how many of each framework's stages sit at each level.

Backbone: our own five kinds of thinking. Bloom: the revised taxonomy. Cognitive: the process each stage exercises (a draft mapping). Mastery: the instructional hierarchy, acquisition to adaptation.

The point: the same 58 stages look different through each lens. GCSE leans on understand and apply; Technical Analysis peaks at connection.

slides.name: The taxonomies underneath

layers.name: SOLO: one idea to beyond the given
Pill SOLO: one idea to beyond the given

params.text: SOLO: one idea to beyond the given
Biggs and Collis (1982): the ladder every framework sits on
Anderson and Krathwohl (2001): Synthesis became Create, above Evaluate
Challenge (X) has no level of its own in Bloom
Six processes across four kinds of knowledge: 24 crossings

slides.notes:
The Taxonomies page, in four pictures.

SOLO is the spine: understanding in five levels, from missing the point to beyond the given. Bloom's revision renamed the levels as verbs and swapped the top two. Our backbone is coarser than Bloom, and Challenge (X) draws on Evaluate's critiquing. And the two-dimensional grid crosses process with kind of knowledge.

Two colour codes, two jobs: blue shades always mean a SOLO level; the other colours mean the kind of thinking.

slides.name: The Analysis tab: SOLO × process

params.text: The Analysis tab  ·  GCSE 2, Describe  ·  illustrative students

Where each answer sits,
and what is missing
One fact, the definitions confused. Missing: the knowledge itself. Reteach first.

layers.name: Each part right, one at a ti

params.text: Each part right, one at a time. Missing: the links. Teach how one part depends on another.

layers.name: Explains it well in talk, mi

params.text: Explains it well in talk, misreads the diagram. Missing: interpretation of the diagram, not the idea.

slides.notes:
For teachers: every stage's Analysis tab places three sample students on a grid of SOLO level against thinking process.

The point is that the same wrong mark means three different things. A needs the knowledge retaught. B has the knowledge and needs the connections. C understands, and has a diagram-reading problem: two formats, two results. Reteaching the content would only help A.

slides.name: Pathways: the engine

params.text: Every answer updates each node, allowing for a slip or a guess.
Dijkstra finds the fastest path to the target, in minutes of teaching.

layers.name: A wrong idea cannot be route

params.text: A wrong idea cannot be routed round. It is fixed before the route goes on.

layers.name: A failure weighs a slip, thi

params.text: A failure weighs a slip, this node, or a gap underneath it: hypotheses to test with the student.
Pathways  ·  the cache question as a network

slides.notes:
Pathways is where the network becomes a route.

Four things it does: traces knowledge from each answer; finds the quickest route (Dijkstra) and the shortest (BFS); refuses to route round a misconception; and when a student fails, asks what most likely went wrong rather than sending them back to the start.

slides.name: How the engine thinks

params.text: P(held | answer) = P·(1−slip) ÷ [P·(1−slip) + (1−P)·guess], then a little learning
Corbett and Anderson (1994). Prior 0.5 · slip 0.1 · guess 0.05 written, 1 in n for multiple choice · learn 0.1 · secure at 0.85

layers.name: A wrong idea counts in full;

params.text: A wrong idea counts in full; exam technique 0.25; a slip 0.2. Absence counts half.
Dijkstra for the quickest; BFS for the fewest steps. A secure step costs a fifth of its time.
P(slip) against P(gap at the node, or a prerequisite)
Bayes over the estimates from before the answer: hypotheses about the answer, not readings of the mind.
Every parameter is the app’s choice, not fitted to data yet, and the estimates do not decay: nothing is yet re-tested after a delay.

slides.notes:
The data science, for the people who'll ask.

Knowledge tracing: Bayesian, Corbett and Anderson 1994. Each answer updates the chance a node is held, allowing for a slip and a guess; a written answer is hard to guess (0.05), a multiple-choice one is 1 in the number of options.

Evidence is weighted by certainty and speed, and now by the teacher's reading of the error.

Routing is Dijkstra over expected minutes: an edge's time divided by the chance of succeeding at it, where representation (verbal, diagram, numeric, trace) is the strongest signal. BFS gives the fewest steps for comparison.

Diagnosis compares a slip against a gap at the node or underneath it. All parameter values are the app's choices, stated, not fitted to data yet. And there's no forgetting: a node marked secure stays secure, so mastery after a delay isn't tested yet. Say this before anyone asks.

slides.name: The evidence underneath

params.text: Then I went looking for evidence
boards: AQA, OCR, Pearson, Cambridge, WJEC
question parts, UK, Singapore and China

slides.notes:
This is The Teaching Model's research. Every examiner report I could find for computer science, split into individual findings: 5,003 of them.

Plus 32 exam papers from the UK, Singapore and China split into 942 question parts, and the 74 student answers the reports publish.

Important caveat to say now: these are findings, not students. A finding is something an examiner wrote. And it's AI-coded: no teacher has checked it yet. We'll come back to that.

slides.name: Act 02 · What I found

params.text: Seven findings. Some confirm what teachers suspect. Some say we have been fixing the wrong thing.

slides.notes: Act two: the findings. This is the heart of the talk. Slow down.

slides.name: Finding 1 · Most mistakes are not wrong ideas

params.text:
mistakes examiners
describe are wrong ideas
670 of 2,191 mistake findings are misconceptions. The other 69% are exam technique, difficulty, slips, vague wording and stopping short.
If that holds for students, reteaching content reaches less than a third of the problem.

params.data:
Kind | Findings
Wrong ideas | 670
Everything else | 1521

slides.notes:
Back to the poll. The answer: about 3 in 10.

Of 2,191 mistake findings, 670 are typed as misconceptions: 31%. Everything else is exam technique, difficulty, slips, imprecise wording, stopping short, not using the scenario.

So when we see a wrong answer and reteach the content, we're aiming at less than a third of what's going wrong.

slides.name: Finding 1 · What the other 69% are

params.data:
Misconceptions, 670
Exam technique, 356
Found difficult, 347
Slips and calculation, 308
Imprecise wording, 186
Stopped short, 164
Not applied to the scenario, 94
Misused the information given, 66

slides.notes:
Read the bars from the top. Misconceptions are the biggest single kind, but they're not the majority.

Exam technique, found difficult and slips together are bigger than misconceptions. Imprecise wording and stopping short are skills, not knowledge.

These are all things a routine can guard against. Hold that thought for act three.

slides.name: Finding 2 · Understanding, not memory

params.text:
Examiners describe understanding
breaking down, not memory
among misconceptions alone: comprehension to recall
The reports usually describe the fact as present but not grasped well enough to keep distinct, or to explain. An observation about answers, not a proof of what students lacked.

slides.notes:
Where the examiners named which step broke, comprehension leads by a long way: 305, then communication 212 and application 165. Recall is 71.

Among the misconceptions alone it's starker: 254 comprehension to 11 recall.

So, if this holds for students, the fix is less often "learn it again" and more often "understand it": contrast it, explain it, use it. These are examiners' descriptions of answers, coded by a model.

params.text: Nodes  ·  Tell these apart, on the Recall tab

layers.name: Kilo and kibi. Bit depth and

params.text: Kilo and kibi. Bit depth and sample rate. Validation and testing. RAM and storage.

slides.notes:
Of the 662 findings that name a wrong idea, almost half (300) are one form: two technically distinct ideas treated as one.

And it shows up in every topic: programming, data representation, computer systems, networks.

One teaching move covers it: teach the pair side by side, with a single test that tells them apart. That's the "Tell these apart" card now on every relevant stage.

slides.name: Finding 4 · The gap is a jump

params.text:
The reported gap is
a jump, not a ladder
Where an examiner shows both the level reached and the level needed, 66 of 98 answers made one point where a connected explanation was needed.

layers.name: Only 17 were a list that fai

params.text: Only 17 were a list that failed to connect.

params.data:
Reached: one point | Needed: connected | 66
Reached: a list | Needed: connected | 17
Reached: one point | Needed: a list | 10
Reached: one point | Needed: beyond | 5

slides.notes:
SOLO terms: unistructural straight to relational, not climbing through multistructural.

66 of 98 findings where both levels can be read: one point, where the question needed a connected explanation. Only 17 were "several points, not connected".

So the step that matters most is from one idea straight to connected ideas. Caveat: both levels are read from one examiner sentence, so they aren't independent.

slides.name: Finding 4 · Why: reasoning

params.text: one-point answers broke down at reasoning, against 12 of 119 at every other level.

The evidence points to a
reason, not more facts.
Nodes  ·  Join it up, on every explain-type stage
p < 0.001, and it holds with any one report left out; an independent subset holds at p = 0.007.

slides.notes:
This points to a cause behind the jump, read from examiner sentences. When an answer stops at one point, the broken step is reasoning in 39 of 68 findings, against 12 of 119 everywhere else.

That holds on the independent subset too (5 of 15 against 7 of 107, p = 0.007).

It's a model reading of examiner sentences, so it points to a reason rather than proving it. In Nodes, every explain-type stage now carries "Join it up": point, because, so, in this case.

slides.name: Finding 5 · Command words promise less

params.text:
Command words promise
less than questions want

params.data:
Identify, 65
State, 58
Give, 47
Describe, 13
Complete, 9
Explain, 0

params.text: % of past questions read as asking for more than the word signals
“Identify” asked for more in 35 of 54 questions.

slides.notes:
The low command words hide a higher demand. Identify, State and Give often want a reason or an example, and the marks show it.

Explain is the honest one: 16 of 16 matched.

So students need to read the marks, not just the word. That's step one of the routine in act three.

slides.name: The command-word dilemma

layers.name: A command word is a promise

params.text:
A command word is a promise
the marks don’t always keep
Command words carry the demand, with published definitions. But Identify asked for more in 65% of questions, State 58%, Give 47%.
Uses command words too (Write, Calculate, Identify), but publishes no mark scheme to check them against.
No command words. Demand is carried by the question type and the marks: single choice, fill in, a worked solution.

layers.name: So: read the marks, not just

params.text: So: read the marks, not just the word. That is step one of the answer routine.

slides.notes:
The dilemma: in the UK, the command word is meant to tell a student how far to go. The evidence says the low words often promise less than the question wants. Explain is the honest one.

Singapore uses command words but publishes no specimen mark schemes, so the promise can't be checked. China doesn't use command words at all: the question type and the marks carry the demand.

So a student who reads only the word is reading the least reliable signal on the page. Teach them to read the marks.

slides.name: Finding 6 · Exams test joining, not transfer

params.text:
The papers test joining ideas.
They almost never test transfer.

layers.name: ask students to join ideas t

params.text: ask students to join ideas together

layers.name: ask them to adapt an idea to

params.text: ask them to adapt an idea to something new
ask outright for transfer to a new context

slides.notes:
Of 495 question parts read for demand: 252 ask students to join ideas, 13 to adapt one, and none to transfer outright.

If exams rarely test transfer, Nodes is where it can be shown. Every stage now has a near and a far transfer item.

slides.name: Finding 7 · Examiners almost never say why

params.text: of mistake findings give any cause: 95 of 2,163.

Reports say what went wrong.
The why has to come from students.

slides.notes:
This one redirected the whole project. Examiners record the error, almost never its cause: 4.4% of mistake findings use any causal wording.

So you can't mine the why from reports. It has to come from students: their answers, contrasts, interviews. Which is exactly what Pathways collects.

slides.notes:
Grouped by meaning, 165 wrong-idea cards fall into 25 themes, and 22 of them appear on two or more boards.

So these are not one board's quirks. A wrong idea about RAM is the same wrong idea at AQA, OCR, Pearson and Cambridge. In Nodes, a wrong idea flagged in one network is now checked first in the others.

slides.name: Three exam systems, side by side

params.text: The paper’s question types; for IT, the standard’s verbs
Partial credit on multiple choice; no credit for working on fill-ins
Weighted by objective (AO1 30 · AO2 40 · AO3 30); a Python lab paper

slides.notes:
The same subject, three very different assessment systems.

UK papers carry demand in command words, mark by points or levels, and come with examiner reports: the 5,003 findings.
China's papers are built from fixed question types, and keys give the answer only. Multiple choice pays partial credit for a correct subset and nothing for any wrong option.
Singapore's are specified by assessment objectives with fixed weights, set with Cambridge, and there is no published mark scheme for the specimens.

None of China or Singapore has examiner reports, so their "what goes wrong" evidence is borrowed from Pearson and Cambridge, and labelled so.

slides.name: What evidence covers which system

params.text: Three comparisons, three kinds of evidence
Every examiner report is from UK boards or international papers taken worldwide. A difficulty seen in the UK cannot be assumed in Singapore or China.

slides.notes:
Three different comparisons need three different kinds of evidence.

Same concepts? The papers answer it, for all three systems. Same reasoning? Papers and mark schemes, and the schemes thin out fast outside the UK. Same difficulties? Only examiner reports or student answers, and there are none for Singapore or China.

So similar demand across countries does not establish similar difficulty. The corpus can't answer the third question yet, and I say so on the site.

slides.notes:
Take one topic, the computer system, and look at every part of the papers on file that assesses it.

The UK asks for names, a sequence, and a part's causal role: the AQA question on main memory in the execute stage is the only one the demand reading says needs reasons.
Singapore asks for the purpose of memory, with no published scheme to say what earns the marks.
Zhejiang asks students to pick the correct statement about a system's hardware, as single choice.

Fetch-decode-execute itself is only assessed in the UK papers here. Same topic, different relationships required, and we can compare the demand, not the difficulty.

slides.name: Why the systems differ

params.text:
Each system is built
for a different job
Several boards set the same qualification, so shared command words, published schemes and examiner reports keep their standards comparable.
One national university-entrance exam: fixed question types and answer keys make marking fast and uniform.
One board, set with Cambridge: the assessment objectives and their weights, not a word, say what is assessed.
An interpretation of how each system is organised, not a finding of the research.

slides.notes:
Why do the systems differ? This is my reading, not a research finding: say so.

The UK has several boards competing to award the same qualification, so it needs a shared vocabulary (command words), published mark schemes and examiner reports to keep standards comparable.

China's Gaokao is a single national university-entrance exam, so it is built for uniform marking at scale: fixed question types and answer keys.

Singapore has one board, set with Cambridge, so the syllabus and its weighted assessment objectives do the specifying.

Each design solves its own problem, and each leaves a different gap for teachers.

slides.name: Act 03 · What it changed

params.text: If 69% of the mistakes examiners describe are not wrong ideas, students need a routine, not only more content.

slides.notes: Act three: what the findings changed in Nodes. From diagnosis to design.

slides.name: The relationship required

params.text:
Which relationship must
the answer establish?
Often seen: the right word, the wrong definition
Often seen: the steps listed, the order unexplained
Often seen: the concept known, applied wrongly
Often seen: the evidence quoted, its significance missing
Often seen: differences listed with no basis
Often seen: a judgement with no “when it holds”
Often seen: relevant points, no conclusion

slides.notes:
The idea that joins everything: not "what SOLO level did they reach?" but "which relationship does the question require, and where does the answer stop satisfying it?"

Seven relationships, from term to precise meaning up to a coherent argument, each with the difficulty examiners typically describe when it fails. Every one of the 58 stages is now tagged with one, and it's on the Question tab.

The tags are my reading of each stage, drafted for Nodes: they need a second reader.

slides.name: Four views of a stage

params.text: What the question requires, beyond its command word
What the mark scheme credits, and what must be explicit
What examiners describe, as observable difficulties

slides.notes:
Every stage now has four views side by side, each from a different source.

What the question demands. What the mark scheme credits, including what has to be explicit. What examiners report, as an observation about answers, which doesn't tell us whether the student lacked knowledge, misread or ran out of time. And the instructional response, which is labelled as a hypothesis.

Only the first three are evidence. The fourth is what to try.

slides.name: The answer routine

params.text: A routine where each step guards one kind of mistake

layers.name: Key terms first; keep the pa

params.text: Key terms first; keep the pairs apart
Point → because → so → in this case
Swap everyday words for technical ones
Endpoints, units, the marks, the question

layers.name: Each share is the part of al

params.text: Each share is the part of all 2,191 mistake findings that step guards against. After marking, log each lost mark by the step that failed.

slides.notes:
This is the design response. Five steps, each guarding one kind of mistake, and together they cover all 2,191 findings.

Decode guards technique and not using the scenario (24%). Retrieve guards misconceptions and difficulty (46%). Reason guards stopping short (7%), but it's the biggest gap by level. Refine guards vague wording (8%). Review guards slips (14%).

It's built on established models: plan, monitor, evaluate (Zimmerman; the EEF guidance), Pólya's look back, self-explanation (Chi), exam wrappers (Lovett). A design to try, not yet tested.

So every stage now has a five-rung ladder, and the teacher records which rung the student reached. Repair only counts later, in a new task, without being asked.

Six of the 58 ladders are the model's own, audited; 52 are drafted under its rules. None is tried with students yet.

slides.name: How sure can we be?

params.text: mistake findings checked by a teacher. Everything here is AI-coded and unvalidated.

layers.name: A finding is an examiner’s s

params.text: A finding is an examiner’s sentence. It says an error is common, not how common.

layers.name: Two AI reviewers agree on de

params.text: Two AI reviewers agree on demand (κ 0.92) and family (κ 0.80): the definitions are clear, not proven right.

layers.name: In the pilot the coder rated

params.text: In the pilot the coder rated its own evidence low on 104 of 138 findings.

slides.notes:
Say this plainly. This is the most important slide for credibility.

No teacher has checked any of these findings yet. The AI reviewers agree with each other, which tells us the definitions are clear, not that the codes are right. And the coder's confidence is mostly low.

The findings are strong leads, consistently presented, and labelled as what they are.

slides.name: Are we reinventing the wheel?

params.text:
Building on the wheel,
not reinventing it
Lewis, Clancy and Vahrenhold (2019), Cambridge Handbook of Computing Education Research, ch. 27: reviews misconceptions and other learning difficulties in computing.

Same: a misconception is one kind of difficulty among others, as we separate wrong ideas from technique, slips and incomplete answers. Different: we mine examiner reports and tie each finding to the mark scheme’s demand.
Two-tier diagnostic tests (Treagust, 1988): a choice, then the reason for it. Concept inventories build distractors from documented misconceptions.
Our revision strand builds on this directly. What is new is where the distractors come from: difficulties examiners reported across boards.
Commercial resources already turn OCR J277 examiner reports into recurring errors and advice.
Ours spans five boards, codes every finding with an evidence level, and separates an observed error from an inferred misconception: only 31% are wrong ideas.
Haberman, Liu and Lee (2019), ETS: models whether the distractor chosen carries information about proficiency.

layers.name: It shows the choice is infor

params.text: It shows the choice is informative, not why it was made. Ours asks the reason, then an option-free reattempt and a new problem: a second study.

slides.notes:
Are we copying, or reinventing the wheel? Neither: each piece has a precedent, and the work builds on them.

The Cambridge Handbook chapter (Lewis, Clancy and Vahrenhold, 2019) reviews research on computing students' misconceptions and learning difficulties, beyond introductory programming. The similarity: it treats a misconception as one kind of learning difficulty among others, which is our separation of wrong ideas from technique, slips and incomplete answers. The difference: it synthesises research; we systematically mine examination reports and link each observation to what the mark scheme demanded.

Choosing an answer and giving a reason goes back to two-tier diagnostic tests (Treagust, 1988). Our revision idea builds on that; the new part is sourcing distractors from what examiners reported across five boards.

And commercial resources already mine OCR reports. The difference is breadth, evidence levels and the line between an observed error and an inferred misconception.

The contribution is the integration and the evidence discipline, not any single piece.

slides.name: How will AI change revision and exams?

params.text: AI, revision and exams  ·  our view

Practice is now abundant.
Understanding is not.

layers.name: A student can answer a hundr

params.text: A student can answer a hundred generated questions by recognising wording or ruling out options, without being able to recall, explain or apply the idea.

layers.name: “A stock answer cued by a ke

params.text: “A stock answer cued by a keyword” is already one of the 25 recurring wrong ideas: fluent text that never meets the question. Generated revision text makes more of it.
The exams test joining, not recognising
In the papers read, 252 of 495 parts ask students to join ideas. Generated practice that drills recognition misses the demand.
The reasoning that cannot be recognised: why the answer is right, why the closest wrong one is wrong, and whether that survives with the options removed.

slides.notes:
How does AI change revision and exams? This is my view, built on the evidence, not a finding of it.

AI has made practice almost free. It hasn't made the thinking free. A student can get through a hundred generated questions by recognising wording, and still not be able to recall, explain or apply.

Fluent but empty text is already a recurring wrong idea in the reports: the stock answer cued by a keyword. Generated revision text produces more of exactly that.

And the exams mostly test joining ideas. So what should hold up in an AI-rich world is the reasoning you can't recognise your way to: why it's right, why the nearest wrong answer is wrong, and whether that holds when the options disappear.

Hypothesis to test: a correct choice made for a weak reason predicts a later transfer failure. The distractor is a design inspired by the evidence, not evidence itself.

slides.notes:
The next strand, as a proposal. Six actions around a multiple-choice question.

Retrieve before the options. Choose. Weigh: name the closest wrong option and why it's tempting, which is the genuinely new step. Justify. Repair after feedback, with the options gone. Transfer to a new problem with the same distinction.

The distractors come from difficulties examiners reported, but a distractor is a design, not evidence: we'd have to test that students find it tempting.

And the hypothesis worth testing: does a correct answer for a weak reason predict a later failure on transfer? That needs real students, under consent.

params.text: The claim to defend: an evidence-traceable method from what these examinations demand, through what examiners report students struggle to show, to teaching responses that can be tested later.

slides.notes:
Two studies, deliberately kept apart.

Study 1 is the documents, and it's what we have now. It can report what's demanded, rewarded and described, as long as it passes three gates: the coverage inventory (done, on the Across systems page), one reconciled demand count (now done: the audit script reproduces 343; the 386 in two earlier reports was written before it was re-run), and a second reader on the relationship codes and on the split between wrong ideas and other mistakes. Until then, it reports the corpus and its limits.

Study 2 is students, under consent. Its hypotheses are written down now, before any data: does the distinction survive without options, and does a right answer for a weak reason predict a transfer failure?

The claim to defend sits underneath both.

One: teacher review, built into the app.
